cues.text: A City Under Siege
In 1472, war over control of the region's lucrative alum mines set Volterra, Italy, against Florence.
Troops under Duke Federico da Montefeltro, hired by Lorenzo de' Medici, stormed the city and subjected it to a brutal sack, notorious in local memory ever since.
A Soldier's Rage
Amid the plundering, a soldier entered the cathedral and made for the tabernacle, seizing a precious ivory pyx that held numerous consecrated Hosts along with other sacred objects.
Accounts differ on exactly what happened next—whether just outside the church or at another point in his flight.
But they agree that, seized by fury against what the pyx contained, the soldier hurled it violently against a stone wall.
Hosts That Rose Into Light
Rather than scattering and falling as ordinary bread would, the consecrated Hosts freed from the shattered pyx rose into the air on their own.
They glowed with an inexplicable light and remained suspended before numerous witnesses for what accounts describe as a considerable length of time.
Some versions of the story add that the soldier himself was struck blind in the moments after his act of violence, restored only when he begged forgiveness and the Hosts were safely recovered.
A Story Told More Than One Way
The surviving sources do not agree on every detail.
Accounts written at different removes from the event vary over which church the pyx was taken from.
They also differ on whether the Hosts rose into the air or were simply found unharmed on the ground.
What remains constant across every version is the core claim: sacrilege met with a visible sign the sack's own violence could not touch.
Legacy
The Volterra account sits within a substantial body of late-medieval Eucharistic tradition built around wartime sacrilege.
Soldiers, plunder, and consecrated objects were treated as loot rather than sacred, yet, in the telling, some visible resistance met the violence.
That resistance could not be overcome.
Whatever the precise original details, the tradition has been kept alive in Volterra for over five centuries as a story less about the soldier's cruelty than about what his cruelty could not undo.
